arXiv:2401.00183v1 [math.AG] 30 Dec 2023

Belyi functions of the special weighted trees of (2,3)(2,3)-type

Nikolai M. Adrianov Note:  Lomonosov Moscow State University, 119991 Moscow, Russia, e-mail: nadrianov@gmail.com    Alexander M. Vatuzov Note:  Lomonosov Moscow State University, 119991 Moscow, Russia, e-mail: amvatuzov@yandex.ru
Abstract

In this paper we calculate the Belyi functions of the weighted trees of (2,3)(2,3)-type with primitive special edge rotation groups. There are 21 Galois orbits of these trees: 6 rational orbits, 12 orbits over quadratic fields, and three orbits over fields of degree 3, 4 and 6. The highest degree of the calculated Belyi function is 32. The calculations are performed using modular functions techniques.

Keywords:  dessins d’enfants, weighted trees, Belyi functions, modular group, modular functions.

Introduction

A dessin d’enfant is a bicolored (connected) graph Γ\Gamma embedded into a compact oriented surface 𝒳{\cal X} in such a way that the complement 𝒳∖Γ{\cal X}\setminus\Gamma is homeomorphic to a disjoint union of open discs. Let XX be a non-singular complex algebraic curve. A function β\beta on XX is called the Belyi function if β\beta has no critical values other than 00, 11 and ∞\infty. Then the preimage β−1​[0,1]\beta^{-1}[0,1] is a dessin d’enfant on XX. The inverse is also true: for an arbitrary dessin d’enfant D=(𝒳,Γ)D=({\cal X},\Gamma) there exists a corresponding Belyi pair (X,β)(X,\beta). Moreover the Belyi pair can be defined over a number field (an algebraic extension of ℚ\mathbb{Q} of finite degree). A detailed introduction into the theory of dessins d’enfants can be found, e.g., in [12].

The action of the Galois group G​a​l​(ℚ¯/ℚ)Gal({\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}/\mathbb{Q}) on the Belyi pairs induces its action on the dessins d’enfants; the orbits of this action are finite. Therefore for any dessin d’enfant the stabilizer under this action is a finite index subgroup of G​a​l​(ℚ¯/ℚ)Gal({\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}/\mathbb{Q}); the correponding number field is called field of moduli of the dessin. For a dessin of genus 0 we put X=ℙ1X=\mathbb{P}^{1} and then its Belyi function β∈ℚ¯​(z)\beta\in{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}(z) is uniquely determined up to a linear fractional substitution z→(a​z+b)/(c​z+d)z\to(az+b)/(cz+d). For all dessins in this paper the Belyi functions can be defined over field of moduli of the dessin; in a general case it is not always possible, see [5].

The degree of a Belyi function is equal to the number of edges of the corresponding dessin. A triple of partitions π⁡(D)=(λ0​|λ1|​λ2)\pi(D)=(\lambda_{0}\,|\,\lambda_{1}\,|\,\lambda_{2}), where λ0,1,2⊢n\lambda_{0,1,2}\vdash n are the partitions constituted by the degrees of black vertices, white vertices and faces of a dessin DD with nn edges, is called the passport of the dessin. In terms of the Belyi pairs, passport describes ramifications of the Belyi function over 00, 11 and ∞\infty. The passport of the dessin is an invariant of the Galois group action.

One can define a dessin DD by a pair of permutations of edges (a,b)(a,b) which correspond to counter-clockwise detours around black and white vertices. The cyclic structures of the permutations aa, bb and a​bab are the components of the passport of the dessin. A group generated by permutations aa and bb is called the edge rotation group and is denoted by E​R​(D)ER(D). The edge rotation group of a dessin is isomorphic to the monodromy group of the cover β:X→ℙ1​(ℂ)\beta:X\to\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C}); it is yet another invariant of the Galois group action.

Example. The ‘‘alien’’ dessin shown in fig. 1 is a dessin d’enfant with 24 edges and the passport (36​16​| 212|​ 211​31)(3^{6}1^{6}\,|\,2^{12}\,|\,21^{1}3^{1}); its edge rotation group is the marvelous Mathieu group 𝐌24\mathrm{\bf M}_{24}, see [22]. The Belyi function of this dessin defined over ℚ⁡(−7)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-7}) is calculated in [21].

A dessin of genus 00 with only one face of degree distinct from 1 is called the weighted tree. Weighted trees can be understood combinatorially as plane trees in which some edges are replaced by multiple ones, see [2], [17]. In [1] weighted trees with special primitive edge rotation groups11 1 A primitive permutation group on nn points is called special if it is different from 𝐂n\mathrm{\bf C}_{n}, 𝐃n\mathrm{\bf D}_{n}, 𝐀n\mathrm{\bf A}_{n} and 𝐒n\mathrm{\bf S}_{n}. are classified. There are 184 such trees, which are subdivided into (at least) 85 Galois orbits and generate 34 primitive groups (the highest degree is 32).

We say that a dessin d’enfant is of (2,3)(2,3)-type if all its black vertices are of degree 1 or 3 and all white vertices are of degree 1 or 2. In other words, the permutations aa and bb are of degree 33 and 22 respectively. In this paper we calculate the Belyi functions for all weighted trees of (2,3)(2,3)-type with special primitive edge rotation groups. There are 43 such trees in 21 Galois orbits; the number of edges varies from 6 up to 32. The Belyi functions for some of them were known before; we used them to test our calculation method. The answers are included here for completeness.

As far as we know, the Belyi functions for orbits 12.4, 12.13, 13.1, 14.2, 17.1, 20.1, 24.2, 32.1 are published for the first time (in [2] the fields of definition for these orbits are given, but not the Belyi functions itself).

Method of calculation

The Belyi function β\beta of a dessin of genus 0 is a rational function in one variable. One can use the passport write down the numerators and denominators of β\beta and β−1\beta-1 as products of polynomials with indeterminate variables. For example, the passport of a weighted tree of (2,3)(2,3)-type with nn edges has the form (3p3​1p1​| 2q2​1q1|​(n−r)1​ 1r)(3^{p_{3}}1^{p_{1}}\,|\,2^{q_{2}}1^{q_{1}}\,|\,(n-r)^{1}\,1^{r}); put the pole of degree n−rn-r at z=∞z=\infty and then the Belyi function takes the form

β=P33⋅P1c​R=Q22⋅Q1c​R+1,\beta=\frac{P_{3}^{3}\cdot P_{1}}{cR}=\frac{Q_{2}^{2}\cdot Q_{1}}{cR}+1, (1)

where c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C} is a constant, P3P_{3}, P1P_{1}, Q2Q_{2}, Q3Q_{3}, R∈ℂ⁡[z]R\in\mathbb{C}[z] are monic polynomials without multiple roots, the degrees of the polynomials are the multiplicities of the passport: deg⁡Pi=pi\deg P_{i}=p_{i}, deg⁡Qi=qi\deg Q_{i}=q_{i}, deg⁡R=r\deg R=r.

The equation (1) gives us a system of non-linear algebraic equations in the coeficients of the polynomials PiP_{i}, QiQ_{i}, RR. The system is underdetermined: there is still a freedom of affine substitution z→A​z+Bz\to Az+B. For (2,3)(2,3)-dessins that appear in the current paper we can add the following two normalization conditions:

the sum of coordinates of the black vertices of degree 3=0,the sum of coordinates of the white vertices of degree 2=1.\begin{array}[]{l}\text{the sum of coordinates of the black vertices of degree 3}=0,\\ \text{the sum of coordinates of the white vertices of degree 2}=1.\end{array} (2)

These conditions set the values of two variables in the system (1):

coeffp3−1​P3=0,coeffq2−1​Q2=−1.\mathrm{coeff}_{p_{3}-1}P_{3}=0,\quad\mathrm{coeff}_{q_{2}-1}Q_{2}=-1. (3)

The most straightforward approach here is to solve the resulting system using the Gröbner bases approach. Unfortunately the complexity of this methods grows rapidly as the number of edges increases; it is practically not applicable for dessins with more than 12 edges.

A more promising approach uses approximate numerical calculations. The general calculation scheme is as follows. We solve the system obtained from (1) and (2) numerically with high enough precision and then express coefficients as algebraic numbers using LLL-algorithm22 2 The abbreviation LLL is made up of the first letters of the names of the authors A. K. Lenstra, H. W. Lenstra, and L. Lovász. In SageMath the algorithm is implemented by algdep function.. This scheme was first used to calculate a Belyi function in [5]. The problem here is to find a good enough starting point such that the Newton method converges to the Belyi function of our dessin33 3 Recall that we write down the system using only the passport of the dessin. Meanwhile the number of the dessins with the given passport can be huge even for a relatively small number of edges.. We use the modular functions method based on ideas from [13] and [20].

Let DD be a (2,3)(2,3)-dessin with nn edges defined by permutations aa, b∈𝐒nb\in\mathrm{\bf S}_{n}. Then the edge rotation group E​R​(D)ER(D) can be presented as a factor of the modular group

Γ=𝐏𝐒𝐋2(ℤ)≃⟨S,T∣S2=(ST)3=1⟩\Gamma=\mathrm{\bf PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})\simeq\langle S,T\mid S^{2}=(ST)^{3}=1\rangle

by a subgroup ΓD⊂Γ\Gamma_{D}\subset\Gamma of index nn. The group Γ\Gamma acts on the completed upper half-plane ℋ∗=ℋ∪ℚ∪{i​∞}{\cal H}^{*}={\cal H}\cup\mathbb{Q}\cup\{i\infty\} defining the well-known tesselation of ℋ∗{\cal H}^{*} by ideal triangles. The fundamental domain of ΓD\Gamma_{D} consists of nn such triangles; it can be easily calculated from aa and bb. We get the commutative triangle

Here J⁡(τ)=11728​j​(τ)J(\tau)=\frac{1}{1728}j(\tau), where j⁡(τ)j(\tau) is a classical modular function invariant under the action of Γ\Gamma. For a dessin DD of genus 00, we have X≃ℙ1X\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1} and the factorization by ΓD\Gamma_{D} is defined by a modular function tD:ℋ→ℙ1t_{D}:\,{\cal H}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} invariant under the action of ΓD\Gamma_{D}.

Let mm be the degree of the pole of β\beta at z=∞=tD​(i​∞)z=\infty=t_{D}(i\infty). Then the function tDt_{D} is invariant under substitution τ→τ+m\tau\to\tau+m and can be expressed via ζ=q1/m=e2​π​i​τ/m\zeta=q^{1/m}=e^{2\pi i\tau/m} and z=tDz=t_{D} has a pole of order 1 at ζ=0\zeta=0. Then the power series expansion of tDt_{D} in variable ζ\zeta takes the form

tD​(ζ)=c−1ζ+c0+∑k=1∞ck​ζk,c−1≠0.t_{D}(\zeta)=\frac{c_{-1}}{\zeta}+c_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}c_{k}\zeta^{k},\quad c_{-1}\neq 0.

Denote by [tD]N​(ζ)[t_{D}]_{N}(\zeta) a partial sum of this expansion:

[tD]N​(ζ)=c−1ζ+c0+∑k=1Nck​ζk.[t_{D}]_{N}(\zeta)=\frac{c_{-1}}{\zeta}+c_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{N}c_{k}\zeta^{k}.

Choose NN points {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} at the boundary of the fundamental domain of ΓD\Gamma_{D}, putting several points for each arc bounding the fundamental domain. Write down the conditions [tD]N(xi)=[tD]N(Mi(xi))][t_{D}]_{N}(x_{i})=[t_{D}]_{N}(M_{i}(x_{i}))], where Mi∈ΓDM_{i}\in\Gamma_{D} is a transformation that defines the pasting of the arc containing xix_{i}. Add the conditions (2) written down in terms of [tD]N[t_{D}]_{N}. We get a system of linear equations of size (N+2)×(N+2)(N+2)\times(N+2); solving it we obtain approximate values for the coefficients {c−1,c0,…​cN}\{c_{-1},c_{0},\ldots c_{N}\}. Substituting the coordinates of the vertices of the triangles of the fundamental domain of ΓD\Gamma_{D} into the approximation of [tD]N[t_{D}]_{N}, we obtain the approximate coordinates for the vertices and of the dessin d’enfant, and thus, the approximate values for coefficients in (1). We use these values as a starting point for the Newton method.

Applying the method described above we have calculated (in almost automatic mode) the Belyi functions of weighted trees of degree up to 32. The method is applicable also to the dessins d’enfants which are not of (2,3)(2,3)-type: any dessin can be reduced to a triangulation and then to a dessin of (2,3)(2,3)-type. However the procedure can increase the number of edges by 6 times, and hence, increase the complexity of the system of algebraic equations. In future works we are going to calculate more Belyi functions and to determine the limits of the method.

At the time of writing, the highest records are the calculations of the Belyi functions with monodromy groups J2J_{2} and C​o3Co_{3} of degree 100 and 276 respectively, see [14], [15]. Similar methods were used in [16] to compute the database of Belyi maps (of degree up to 9).

Results of calculation

In this section we present the list of calculated Belyi functions. We try to write down the Belyi functions in a most compact way (orienting to the amazing classical formulas by F. Klein).

In (1) we placed the only pole of degree >1>1 to the point z=∞z=\infty. This leaves us a freedom of affine substitutions z→A​z+Bz\to Az+B. For a weighted tree with only one face of degree 1 we place the second pole at the point z=0z=0. In all other cases we take the second leading coefficient of the polynomial P3P_{3}, P1P_{1}, Q2Q_{2}, Q1Q_{1} or of the numerator of the Belyi function and assign it to zero. Our choice of the polynomial here is more or less arbitrary.

There is still a freedom of multiplicative substitution z→A​zz\to Az. We choose the value of AA in such a way that

  1. (1)

    the leading coefficients of P3P_{3}, P1P_{1}, Q2Q_{2}, Q1Q_{1} and RR are equal to 11 (in several cases we get more compact formulas if we allow the polynomial RR to be non-monic);

  2. (2)

    all other coefficients are integer algebraic numbers (the smallest possible with respect to the norm).

We get into a trouble with this procedure only for the orbit 32.1 when the coefficients have non-unique factorization. Is there a proper way to construct a minimal model of the Belyi function? It is an interesting question.

An ordinary tree (orbit 13.1, see [1]), the orbit consists of four dessins, see fig. 17. In [4] a one-parameter family of Zolotarev polynomials55 5 Zolotarev polynomial is a complex polynomial with three finite critical values. Zolotarev polynomials relate to Shabat polynomials in the same way as Fried pairs (covers of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} ramified over four points) relate to Belyi pairs. is calculated. The Shabat polynomial of this plane tree can be obtained from the family of Zolotarev polynomials by specializing its parameter TT.

The field of definition of the Shabat polynomials turns out to be the same as the field of definition of the family of Zolotarev polynomials. it can be defined as K=ℚ⁡(a)K=\mathbb{Q}(a), where a4+13​a2+13=0a^{4}+13a^{2}+13=0. Note that ε=(a2+2)/3\varepsilon=(a^{2}+2)/3 satisfies ε2+3​ε−1=0\varepsilon^{2}+3\varepsilon-1=0, i.e. it is a unity of the field.

The Galois group of the field KK is cyclic of order 4, and hence it contains all the roots of the equation a4+13​a2+13=0a^{4}+13a^{2}+13=0; the roots are {a,a/ε,−a,−a/ε}\{a,a/\varepsilon,-a,-a/\varepsilon\}.

n=32n=32, (310​12​| 212​18|​ 311​11)(3^{10}1^{2}\,|\,2^{12}1^{8}\,|\,31^{1}1^{1}), E​R=𝐀𝐒𝐋5​(2)ER=\mathrm{\bf ASL}_{5}(2)

A weighted tree (orbit 32.1, see [1]), the orbit consists of 6 dessins, see fig. 24.

One can use GAP66 6 https://www.gap-system.org/ to check that there exist 6 conjugacy classes of elements of order 31 in 𝐀𝐒𝐋5​(2)\mathrm{\bf ASL}_{5}(2). For any two of then C1C_{1}, C2C_{2} there exists k∈(ℤ/31​ℤ)∗k\in(\mathbb{Z}/31\mathbb{Z})^{*} such that any element of C1C_{1} is the kk-th power of an element of C2C_{2}. There are 6 irrational numbers among the values of irreducible characters on these classes; they are of the form e31k+e312​k+e314​k+e318​k+e3116​ke^{k}_{31}+e_{31}^{2k}+e_{31}^{4k}+e_{31}^{8k}+e_{31}^{16k}, where e31e_{31} is a primitive root of unity of degree 31. The numbers are the roots of the polynomial a6+a5+3​a4+11​a3+44​a2+36​a+32a^{6}+a^{5}+3a^{4}+11a^{3}+44a^{2}+36a+32. The Galois group of the polynomial is cyclic of order 6.

It follows from the general theory that the Belyi functions of these dessins are defined over the splitting field of a6+a5+3​a4+11​a3+44​a2+36​a+32a^{6}+a^{5}+3a^{4}+11a^{3}+44a^{2}+36a+32; our calculations confirm it. This field of definition was also calculated in 2016 by J. Voight. The formulas of the Belyi function are too unwieldy to bring them here; there reader can find them in the supplementary materials.

Supplementary materials. The Belyi functions presented in this paper are available as SageMath files in the GitHub repository https://github.com/nadrianov/supplementary.
